First differences in predicted probabilities

Source: R/qoi.R
first_difference.Rd

The change in the predicted probability of every alternative when a covariate moves from from to to, holding the other covariates at a profile (the estimation cases' weighted means and modes; the default in the wide layout), at a supplied one-case newdata, or averaged over the estimation cases (average = TRUE, the average first difference / average marginal effect; the default in the long layout). Intervals by the delta method (numerical Jacobian of the quantity with respect to the parameters) or by simulation from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates (the practice of Bagozzi and Marchetti 2017; this is not a bootstrap). A fit with an offset carries it along: the estimation offsets for average = TRUE, their weighted mean at a profile, and offset must be given with newdata. For a fixed-effects fit the profile holds the unit constants at the modal unit's values, an arbitrary choice in a balanced panel: average = TRUE (the effect averaged over the estimation cases and their units) is the usual quantity there.

Usage

first_difference(
  object,
  var,
  from,
  to,
  newdata = NULL,
  average = NULL,
  alternative = NULL,
  type = c("prob", "prob_outcome", "regime"),
  stage = c("both", "outcome", "inflation"),
  ci = c("delta", "sim", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  R = 1000,
  offset = NULL
)

Arguments

object

A "choicemodel" fit.

var

Name of the covariate to change.

from, to

Its two values (a factor level for a factor).

newdata

Optional data frame giving the profile (one case: one row in the wide layout, that case's rows in the long layout).

average

If TRUE, average the first differences over the estimation cases (weighted by the frequency weights). NULL (default) means FALSE in the wide layout (a profile) and TRUE in the long layout, where there is no natural one-case profile.

alternative

Long layout: the alternative whose rows receive the change (for an alternative-specific covariate); NULL changes all rows.

type

"prob" (default), "prob_outcome", or "regime" (inflated models).

stage

"both" (default), "outcome", or "inflation": which equation(s) see the change (inflated models).

ci

"delta" (default), "sim" (simulation from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates), or "none".

level

Confidence level.

R

Number of simulation draws for ci = "sim".

offset

Offset for newdata when the fit has one (an n x J matrix in the wide layout, a vector aligned to the rows in the long layout).

Value

A data frame of class "pc_fd" with one row per alternative (for type = "regime", one row per regime: one with a single inflated alternative, the choice regime and each captive regime with several): from and to are the predicted probabilities at the two covariate values, diff their difference, and lower, upper the interval for diff.

Details

For inflated models, type = "prob" moves the probabilities of the observed alternatives (regime mixture included) and type = "prob_outcome" the outcome-stage probabilities, that is, the effects among cases in the choice regime, which is what Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) report when comparing BIMNL with MNL effects; type = "regime" reports the change in \(P(s = 1)\) (with several inflated alternatives, the probabilities of the choice regime and of captivity to each). stage restricts the covariate change to one equation when the covariate enters both: with stage = "outcome" the covariate moves in the outcome equations while the split equation keeps it at from, and conversely for "inflation". The two stage effects need not add up to the total ("both"): the mixture is nonlinear, so the remainder is an interaction of the two changes.

In the long layout the covariate is changed on every row (a case-specific covariate) or only on the rows of one alternative (alternative =, for an alternative-specific covariate), and average = TRUE is the default since there is no natural one-case profile.

References

Bagozzi, B.E. and Marchetti, K. (2017). Distinguishing occasional abstention from routine indifference in models of vote choice. Political Science Research and Methods, 5(2), 277-294. doi:10.1017/psrm.2015.42

See also

predict.choicemodel(), rrr()

Other quantities of interest: rrr()

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- rmnl(1000, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5)))
m <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)
first_difference(m, "x1", 0, 1)
#> First differences: x1 from 0 to 1 at the covariate profile (delta intervals at 95%)
#>  alternative  from    to   diff  lower  upper
#>            a 0.271 0.324  0.053  0.018  0.089
#>            b 0.471 0.200 -0.271 -0.303 -0.239
#>            c 0.258 0.475  0.218  0.176  0.259
first_difference(m, "x1", 0, 1, average = TRUE, ci = "sim", R = 500)
#> First differences: x1 from 0 to 1, averaged over the estimation cases (simulation (R=500) intervals at 95%)
#>  alternative  from    to   diff  lower  upper
#>            a 0.254 0.299  0.045  0.012  0.081
#>            b 0.474 0.238 -0.236 -0.264 -0.208
#>            c 0.271 0.463  0.191  0.153  0.232
